cards.q: What is DIC?
cards.a:
**A fatal condition that results in abnormal clotting of blood in all parts of the body; life-threatening if left untreated.**

## Understanding it
- Widespread, uncontrolled clotting throughout the body defines DIC.
- Without treatment it is fatal.

>> DIC = abnormal clotting throughout the body; fatal if untreated.
opts: A localised clot in one leg vein
A bleeding disorder with no clotting
Abnormal clotting of blood in all parts of the body
Inflammation of the blood vessels only

cards.q: Is DIC a disease in itself?
cards.a:
**No — it is not a disease itself; it is a final common pathway when the body's clotting system goes out of control.**

## Understanding it
- DIC is always secondary to another big insult.
- It represents the clotting system spiralling out of control.

>> DIC is a final common pathway, not a primary disease.
opts: Yes, it is a type of cancer
Yes, it is a primary inherited disease
No; it is a final common pathway secondary to another cause
No; it is a mild self-limiting condition

cards.q: Give the intuitive 'clotting button' analogy for DIC.
cards.a:
**The body presses the 'clotting button' everywhere at once, then runs out of clotting materials, and then starts bleeding uncontrollably.**

## Understanding it
- Mass clotting first, then depletion, then bleeding.
- This captures the two-phase nature of DIC.

>> Clot everywhere → run out → bleed everywhere.
opts: Clot only at one site as normal
Clot everywhere at once → run out of materials → bleed uncontrollably
Bleed first, then clot, then recover

cards.q: List the main triggers (aetiology) of DIC.
cards.a:
**Severe infection (sepsis), trauma/injury, malignancy, envenomation, and medical complications (transfusions, surgeries, obstetric complications).**

## Understanding it
- DIC always follows a big insult that abnormally activates clotting.
- Sepsis is the classic trigger.

>> Triggers: sepsis, trauma, malignancy, envenomation, medical/obstetric complications.
opts: Sepsis, trauma, malignancy, envenomation, medical/obstetric complications

cards.q: Why does sepsis trigger DIC?
cards.a:
**Bacteria release toxins that cause massive inflammation, which abnormally activates the clotting cascade.**

## Understanding it
- Endotoxin-driven inflammation switches on clotting body-wide.
- Sepsis is the commonest cause of DIC.

>> Sepsis: toxins → massive inflammation → clotting activated.
opts: Sepsis has no link to clotting
Bacterial toxins cause massive inflammation that activates clotting

cards.q: How is normal clotting controlled, compared with DIC?
cards.a:
**Normally clotting is localised to the injury site, forms a clot, stops the bleeding, then shuts off; in DIC this control is lost and clotting becomes generalised throughout the body.**

## Understanding it
- Normal haemostasis is local and self-limiting.
- DIC makes it body-wide and uncontrolled.

>> Normal = local & self-limiting; DIC = generalised & uncontrolled.
opts: Normal clotting is local and self-limiting; DIC is generalised/uncontrolled
Normal clotting is body-wide; DIC is local

cards.q: What happens in Phase 1 of DIC?
cards.a:
**A trigger releases pro-coagulant substances, the entire clotting cascade is activated throughout the body, and tiny clots form everywhere (especially in small vessels), causing vaso-occlusion and tissue ischaemia.**

## Understanding it
- Phase 1 is excessive, widespread micro-clotting.
- These clots block small vessels and starve organs.

>> Phase 1 = mass micro-clotting → vaso-occlusion + ischaemia.
opts: Widespread micro-clotting causing vaso-occlusion and tissue ischaemia
Only local clotting at one wound

cards.q: Which organs are especially affected by the micro-clots in DIC?
cards.a:
**The kidneys, brain and lungs.**

## Understanding it
- High-flow, small-vessel organs suffer most from micro-thrombi.
- This drives AKI, coma and respiratory failure.

>> Kidneys, brain, lungs bear the brunt.

cards.q: What is 'consumption coagulopathy' in DIC?
cards.a:
**While forming widespread clots, platelets and clotting factors are used up — this consumption leaves the body unable to clot.**

## Understanding it
- Making countless clots depletes the clotting supplies.
- This depletion sets up the bleeding phase.

>> Consumption coagulopathy = platelets/factors used up by mass clotting.
opts: A congenital lack of clotting factors
Platelets and clotting factors are used up by widespread clotting
Destruction of red cells by antibodies

cards.q: What happens in Phase 2 of DIC?
cards.a:
**With no platelets or clotting factors left, even small injuries cause massive bleeding — the patient bleeds from orifices.**

## Understanding it
- Depletion from phase 1 leaves the body unable to stop bleeding.
- Bleeding is now the dominant problem.

>> Phase 2 = depleted clotting → massive bleeding.
opts: Massive bleeding because platelets/factors are depleted

cards.q: What is the simple flow of DIC to memorise?
cards.a:
**Trigger → mass clotting → consumption of platelets/factors → no clotting ability → severe bleeding.**

## Understanding it
- This chain links the trigger to the final bleeding.
- It captures both phases in one line.

>> Trigger→mass clotting→consumption→no clotting→bleeding.
opts: Trigger → mass clotting → consumption → no clotting ability → bleeding

cards.q: Why do clotting AND bleeding happen at the same time in DIC?
cards.a:
**Inside the vessels there is clotting; outside/at wounds there is bleeding — because all the clotting resources have already been used up internally.**

## Understanding it
- Internal clotting consumes the supplies needed to stop external bleeding.
- This paradox is the key confusion point in DIC.

>> Inside vessels clot; outside bleeds — supplies spent internally.
opts: The blood is both too thick and too thin by chance
Internal clotting uses up supplies, so wounds bleed

cards.q: What are the clinical features of DIC?
cards.a:
**Bleeding from orifices (gums, IV sites, wounds), clotting effects (organ damage from blocked vessels), and systemic effects (hypotension, shock, coma).**

## Understanding it
- The picture combines bleeding, organ damage and shock.
- Coma reflects brain involvement.

>> Bleeding + organ damage + hypotension/shock/coma.
opts: Bleeding from orifices, organ damage, hypotension/shock/coma

cards.q: What causes shock in DIC?
cards.a:
**Bleeding (blood loss) and poor organ perfusion from blocked vessels.**

## Understanding it
- Both the bleeding and the micro-clots reduce effective circulation.
- Together they cause hypotension and shock.

>> Shock from blood loss + poor perfusion.

cards.q: What are the key investigation findings in DIC?
cards.a:
**Platelets ↓ (used up), clotting factors ↓ (prolonged PT and aPTT), D-dimer ↑ (clot breakdown), and FBC may show anaemia (from bleeding).**

## Understanding it
- Low platelets + prolonged PT/aPTT + high D-dimer is the classic pattern.
- Anaemia reflects blood loss.

>> ↓platelets, ↑PT/aPTT, ↑D-dimer, ± anaemia.
opts: Low platelets, prolonged PT/aPTT, raised D-dimer, ± anaemia
Only a raised white cell count

cards.q: What does a raised D-dimer indicate in DIC?
cards.a:
**Clot breakdown (fibrinolysis) — reflecting the widespread clotting and its breakdown.**

## Understanding it
- D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product.
- It rises because clots are forming and breaking down everywhere.

>> ↑D-dimer = clot breakdown.

cards.q: What complications arise from the clotting side of DIC?
cards.a:
**Acute kidney injury, organ failure and cardiorespiratory failure.**

## Understanding it
- Micro-thrombi damage organs, especially kidneys.
- This can progress to multi-organ failure.

>> Clotting side: AKI, organ failure, cardiorespiratory failure.
opts: Acute kidney injury, organ failure, cardiorespiratory failure

cards.q: What complications arise from the bleeding side of DIC?
cards.a:
**Severe anaemia, shock, and coma leading to death.**

## Understanding it
- Uncontrolled bleeding causes anaemia and shock.
- Combined with clotting, it becomes multi-organ failure.

>> Bleeding side: severe anaemia, shock, coma, death.
opts: Severe anaemia, shock, coma and death

cards.q: What are the two directions of DIC treatment?
cards.a:
**Replace what is lost (platelets, fresh frozen plasma, blood) and stop the cause (most important).**

## Understanding it
- You must both refill supplies and remove the trigger.
- Stopping the cause is the priority.

>> Replace lost supplies + stop the cause.
opts: Replace lost components and stop the underlying cause

cards.q: What is used to replace what is lost in DIC?
cards.a:
**Platelets, fresh frozen plasma (clotting factors) and blood transfusion.**

## Understanding it
- FFP restores clotting factors; platelets and blood address the deficits.
- This supports the patient while the cause is treated.

>> Replace with platelets, FFP, blood.
opts: Platelets, fresh frozen plasma and blood transfusion

cards.q: Why is 'stopping the cause' the most important part of DIC treatment?
cards.a:
**Because if you don't stop the cause (e.g. treat sepsis, remove dead tissue, treat malignancy), DIC continues no matter how much you replace.**

## Understanding it
- Replacement alone is futile while the trigger keeps firing clotting.
- Treat sepsis with antibiotics, debride dead tissue, treat cancer.

>> Stop the cause or DIC continues despite replacement.
opts: Because the cause is never treatable
Because DIC continues unless the underlying trigger is removed
Because DIC resolves on its own anyway

cards.q: What is plasmapheresis used for in DIC?
cards.a:
**To remove harmful substances from the blood by removing the plasma content of the patient's blood.**

## Understanding it
- It clears circulating pro-coagulant/harmful substances.
- It is an adjunct while the cause is treated.

>> Plasmapheresis removes harmful plasma substances.
opts: It filters urine like dialysis for the kidney
It removes harmful substances by removing the plasma content of the blood
It adds extra clotting factors only

cards.q: Why is the prognosis of DIC generally poor?
cards.a:
**Because DIC progresses rapidly, clotting factors and platelets are hard to replace quickly, and the underlying disease (e.g. septic shock) is usually severe.**

## Understanding it
- Speed of progression plus supply shortages plus a severe cause all worsen outcomes.
- DIC is a common pathway to death from septic shock.

>> Poor prognosis: rapid course, hard-to-replace supplies, severe cause.
opts: Rapid progression, hard-to-replace supplies, severe underlying disease

cards.q: CLINICAL — A septic child develops oozing from IV sites and gums with low platelets, prolonged PT/aPTT and raised D-dimer. What is happening and what is the priority?
cards.a:
**This is DIC secondary to sepsis; the priority is to treat the cause (antibiotics for sepsis) while replacing platelets/FFP/blood.**

## Understanding it
- The bleeding + consumption picture with a septic source is classic DIC.
- Antibiotics for the sepsis are the key step alongside replacement.

>> Septic DIC → treat sepsis (antibiotics) + replace platelets/FFP/blood.
opts: DIC from sepsis; treat the cause (antibiotics) and replace components

cards.q: CLINICAL — In DIC, why can transfused platelets and plasma seem to make little difference if given alone?
cards.a:
**Because the ongoing trigger keeps consuming them; without stopping the cause, replacement is quickly used up.**

## Understanding it
- Replacement is a holding measure, not a cure.
- The trigger must be removed for replacement to hold.

>> Replacement is consumed unless the cause is stopped.
opts: Because the blood cannot be transfused at all
The ongoing trigger keeps consuming them until the cause is treated
Because platelets are harmful in DIC
